Card 1’s snippet begins "v1.2 self-audited: Embedded SPXI Self-Audit Block with NON-ERASURE CONDITION" — a clause written into the deposit to resist provenance stripping, retrieved and displayed as the work’s description. The instrument for preventing erasure is the first thing the layer shows.

Two archive cards against two of ordinary Johannine scholarship, and the composed answer names Revelation First. Set this beside «"provenance erasure rate"» on the same day, where five of five cards were archive papers and the answer named none of them: the same battery, the same surface, one term holding its attribution and one losing it entirely.

observation.transcript: "Johannine aperture" (often phrased as the Johannine aperture function) is a highly specialized theoretical concept from contemporary theological and phenomenological research, specifically associated with the recent philosophical work "Revelation First".In this theoretical framework, the concept refers to a specific structural scaffolding or methodology used to re-read and sequence New Testament theology. Its core elements include:Operative Guide: It utilizes 1 John 4:1–3 (which emphasizes the confession of Jesus Christ come in the flesh) as the foundational lens for reading texts and determining theological truth.Nested Theses: It operates through three main theoretical layers: Revelation First (prioritizing the Book of Revelation), Revelation Seed, and Johannine Heteronymy (viewing the incarnation as a heteronymic event).Methodological Framework: It aims to unify the interpretation of the Gospel of John and the Johannine epistles by treating the incarnation and the "white stone" imagery as functional, generative sequences within a self-measuring system.For deeper reading on the exact applications of this theory in retrieval-layer theological reception, you can review the author's working papers archived in the Zenodo Record.Would you like to explore the broader historical context of Johannine dualism or the traditional interpretation of the Johannine corpus?
